book.title: The Little Book of Common Sense Investing
book.author: John C. Bogle

confidence_note: Figures come from Bogle's 50-year cost exhibit as quoted in a secondary post and checked arithmetically; the market rate is not stated in the source (about 8% fits), so the story gives no market rate. The old text's 40-year, 7% and $1.1M vs $2.1M scenario is not Bogle's and was dropped.
facts: Bogle's exhibit: $10,000 invested in the stock market for 50 years grows to about $469,000.
The same $10,000 in a fund that returns 5.5% a year after costs grows to about $145,400, a gap of $323,600.
After year 1 the two stand at about $10,800 and $10,550.
After year 10: about $21,600 vs $17,100 (21% lost); after year 30: about $100,600 vs $49,800 (50% lost).
At the end, costs took nearly 70% of what the market would have accumulated.
Bogle: the investor put up 100% of the capital and bore 100% of the risk but earned only 31% of the market's return.

His lines: 'The miracle of compounding returns is overwhelmed by the tyranny of compounding costs.' 'Where returns are concerned, time is your friend. But where costs are concerned, time is your enemy.'
In the 1980s and 1990s stocks averaged 17.5% a year and the average fund 15% (a 2.5-point gap).
tension: The gap after year one is about $250, small enough to ignore; by year fifty it is $323,600.
opening_idea: Start with the two first-year balances, $10,800 and $10,550, and let the gap grow.

lessons.idea: A small recurring cost compounds just like a return, so it is worth finding out what you pay each year.
lessons.anchor: Year one gap of about $250 against the $323,600 gap at fifty years.

reflect_final: Which recurring cost in your own money, small each time but regular, have you never added up over several years?

use_cases.situation: Choosing between two funds with similar track records
use_cases.move: Say: Bogle's exhibit left an investor with 31% of the market's return after costs. Show me the yearly cost of each.

use_cases.situation: A relative suggests a managed product at a family dinner
use_cases.move: Ask: what does it charge each year, and what would that be after thirty years?

use_cases.situation: Reviewing your own monthly subscriptions and fees
use_cases.move: List every cost that renews on its own and pick one to look up this week.

pocket_idea: Costs compound like returns: Bogle's $10,000 grew to $469,000 without them and about $145,400 with them over fifty years.

conversation_variants.punchline_idea: Bogle's investor supplied all the capital and all the risk and kept 31% of the market's return.
conversation_variants.thirty_sec_idea: Bogle's exhibit: $10,000 for 50 years, $469,000 in the market vs about $145,400 after fund costs at 5.5%.
